cards.title: DeepSeek V4 Flash: 304B params, budget pricing

panels.head: A 304B-parameter model that costs less than GPT-4o Mini
panels.sub: DeepSeek V4 Flash (0731) lands at $0.14/M input and $0.27/M output tokens — undercutting most frontier models while claiming top-tier intelligence scores.

panels.head: Beats MiniMax M3, a model 40% larger
panels.sub: Artificial Analysis ranks it above MiniMax M3 (428B parameters) on its Intelligence Index, meaning raw parameter count is a poor proxy for capability here.

panels.head: Default reasoning level undersells it
panels.sub: At default reasoning effort the outputs can look mediocre. Switching to high reasoning effort via OpenRouter produced visibly stronger results in Simon Willison's tests.

panels.head: "Substantially enhanced agentic capabilities" is the headline feature
panels.sub: DeepSeek positions this as an agent-first model. At 167 GB it's self-hostable on a well-specced server, which matters for regulated deployments that can't route data through third-party APIs.

panels.head: Best cost-per-intelligence ratio on the market right now
panels.sub: If you're running high-volume agentic workflows — document parsing, multi-step CV pipelines, edge-orchestration tasks — this is worth a bench run before committing to pricier alternatives. Always set reasoning_effort high in tests.

cards.title: MarbleOS bets agents need GUIs, not chat boxes

panels.head: AI agents are stuck at the command-line stage
panels.sub: Even in natural language, you still have to remember what an agent can do and how to ask for it — /skill-name [param1] [param2] is just a terminal flag with nicer syntax.

panels.head: The 1984 Mac didn't add power — it made existing power visible
panels.sub: Xerox PARC's insight was that capabilities people can see get used far more than capabilities they must recall. MarbleOS is applying that same logic to agentic workflows.

panels.head: Tasks become cards; tools appear before the job runs
panels.sub: Each delegated job sits on a kanban-style board. Marble surfaces which tools it plans to invoke before execution, and delivers a direct artifact — spreadsheet, deck, file — not a buried transcript.

panels.head: Visible tooling prompts delegation people wouldn't attempt via chat
panels.sub: The team reports that when users can see available actions, they assign tasks they'd never have typed into a blank box — suggesting the interface itself shapes perceived agent utility.

panels.head: For PMs building agent products: discoverability is a design problem
panels.sub: If your agent's capabilities are invisible, adoption will track ChatGPT power-users only. MarbleOS is a live beta worth testing as a reference point for how surface-level tool visibility changes user behaviour.

cards.title: Microsoft's Flint: charts from plain-language specs

panels.head: Charting libraries want code. Most insights live in prose.
panels.sub: Every time an analyst or PM wants a custom chart, they either wrangle D3/Vega configs or wait for an engineer. Flint bets there's a better interface layer.

panels.head: Flint is a declarative visualization language designed to be written — or generated — by LLMs.
panels.sub: Instead of imperative chart code, you describe what you want in a structured natural-language-friendly spec. The renderer handles the rest.

panels.head: Specs map data fields to visual channels with minimal boilerplate.
panels.sub: Flint sits between 'just ask GPT' and a full grammar-of-graphics system — intentionally constrained so an LLM can produce correct output reliably rather than hallucinating chart configs.

panels.head: LLM-friendly grammars could replace brittle chart-generation prompts.
panels.sub: Current AI chart generation often outputs broken Vega-Lite or matplotlib. A purpose-built target grammar gives models a smaller, more predictable output space — higher first-pass correctness.

panels.head: If you're building agentic dashboards or report-gen pipelines, watch this spec.
panels.sub: A stable, LLM-writable chart language is the missing plumbing between natural-language data queries and rendered visuals in operator-facing tools. Flint is an early bet on that layer from Microsoft Research.

cards.title: MCP 2.0 drops session state — one request does it all

panels.head: MCP 2.0 cuts tool calls from two HTTP requests to one
panels.sub: The 2026-07-28 spec drops the session-init handshake entirely. Client metadata now travels in the single POST body, and a method header replaces the old Mcp-Session-Id dance.

panels.head: Stateless design means no server-side session routing headaches
panels.sub: Legacy MCP required sticky sessions — every follow-up request had to hit the same backend instance. Stateless MCP servers are now trivially horizontally scalable and far easier to audit.

panels.head: MCP tools are controllable enough for on-device models
panels.sub: Handing an agent a shell and curl is powerful but risky and demands a frontier model. Discrete, typed MCP tools are auditable, scope-limited, and workable for laptop-sized models — a real edge-compute angle.

panels.head: mcp-explorer: a zero-install CLI for probing any MCP server
panels.sub: Built with Codex in a day, it lists and calls tools on any stateless MCP endpoint without a local install. A concrete example of how much easier the new spec makes client-side tooling.

panels.head: Stateless MCP is the right primitive for controlled AI tooling in regulated environments
panels.sub: If you're deploying agents in settings where every tool call must be logged and scoped — medical imaging, industrial inspection, fintech — stateless MCP gives you an auditable, versioned interface without the orchestration overhead of a full shell agent.

cards.title: Your phone already wrote today's journal entry

panels.head: A blank page killed journaling for you
panels.sub: Your phone tracked your route, photos, workouts, calendar, and music all day — but your journal app still opens to nothing. The data exists; nobody stitches it into prose.

panels.head: Anyone who opens their camera roll 6 months later and can't remember why they took the photo
panels.sub: The frustration is common enough to have spawned dozens of near-identical threads. It spikes around travel, new-parent milestones, and annual review season — high-emotion moments where people most want a record and least have energy to write one.

panels.head: A first draft is already waiting when you open the app
panels.sub: On-device LLM weaves GPS stops, photos, activity rings, and calendar events into a readable narrative. You confirm, trim, or add one or two things the data can't know. A 'trip mode' builds each day silently in the background and exports the whole journey as a printable book.

panels.head: Apple Journal, Day One, Notion: all blank-page tools with attachment bolted on
panels.sub: They store your data but don't synthesise it. The closest competitors (Rewind, Saga) lean on cloud processing and broad data capture — exactly the privacy posture that makes a journal feel unsafe. An on-device-first approach is a genuine differentiator, not just a checkbox.

panels.head: Hypothesis: people will grant location + photo access if the output feels private
panels.sub: Test it cheap: post a 60-second demo of a GPT-4o prompt turning a fake day's metadata into a paragraph, add a waitlist link, and measure sign-ups. Search 'journaling app' on r/LifeProTips and r/SomebodyMakeThis for duplicate requests to size the demand before writing a line of code.

cards.title: smevals: run model evals in four commands
cards.caption: smevals separates run, grade, and serve into discrete steps — so you can re-grade old runs against new checks without re-hitting the API.

script.text: # smevals — outputs full README to stdout for your coding agent to read
# Agent scaffolds eval/ directory with YAML task files
uvx smevals run eval/ -m gpt-5.5 -m claude-opus-4.6
Running 12 tasks × 2 configs → 24 runs saved to eval/runs/

cards.title: Datasette Agent can now run JS in the browser

panels.head: An AI agent that reaches into your browser tab
panels.sub: Datasette Agent 0.4a0 ships a new primitive: agent tools can now execute arbitrary JavaScript directly inside the user's browser, not just on the server.

panels.head: Datasette Agent wraps an LLM around your SQLite data
panels.sub: The project lets you query, explore, and act on Datasette instances through a chat interface. Plugins expose 'tools' the model can invoke — until now those tools only ran server-side.

panels.head: await context.browser_task() is the new primitive
panels.sub: Plugin authors call this method from any tool handler; the agent runtime serialises the JS payload and runs it in the active browser session. No separate browser-automation stack required.

panels.head: Client-side state is now fair game for agentic workflows
panels.sub: Tools can now read DOM state, manipulate charts, trigger client-rendered UI, or export data the server never sees — closing the gap between 'chat with your data' and 'act on your data'.

panels.head: A low-friction pattern for browser-aware agent plugins
panels.sub: If you're building internal data tools on Datasette, this is the cheapest path to agents that can both query a database and drive the front-end — worth tracking as the alpha stabilises.

cards.title: Fuzzy search ate exact match — users are angry

panels.head: "Fuzzy search ate my exact result"
panels.sub: A 76-upvote HN thread: developers and power users are furious that exact-match search has been quietly removed or buried across tools, internal wikis, SaaS products, and community platforms.

panels.head: Anyone searching a large corpus by precise string
panels.sub: Support agents looking up ticket IDs, engineers grepping docs, ops staff finding exact SKUs or error codes — fuzzy matching returns noise when you already know the term.

panels.head: A search widget that defaults to exact, degrades gracefully
panels.sub: Drop-in search component (JS library or SaaS API) that runs exact match first, shows fuzzy results in a collapsible secondary section. Integrates with existing backends — Elasticsearch, Typesense, Postgres full-text.

panels.head: Algolia, Typesense, and friends bury exact-match controls
panels.sub: Most libraries support exact matching via query flags, but the default UX exposes none of it. Operators have to hand-tune relevance weights and add custom UI — work most product teams skip.

panels.head: Search HN and Reddit for "exact match search" frustration threads
panels.sub: If duplicates are frequent and recent, build a one-page landing page targeting the query "add exact match to site search" and measure signups before writing a line of code.
